items.text: I agree with Misti Y-- that you can love Cirque shows generally and still not like Le Reve. But that is a separate conversation. For me, the theatre and visual design are the strongest parts. The scenery and decor are stunning start to finish. The whole concept is beautiful. However, it doesn't translate well to live performance. The storyline is not especially entertaining, and when I went to see it, the stage kept malfunctioning. That makes it hard to stay engaged, even in the impressive scenes. The show seems to try to reach the flair and spectacle that Cirque is known for, but it doesn't quite get there. I would go to see Le Reve mostly to experience that beautiful theatre. Otherwise, you may be better off spending your money on other shows.

I'm with Misty on this, and I think there are plenty of people who love Cirque shows but still aren't crazy about Le Reve. That's a separate discussion though. For me, the theatre, the set, the design, is the best part of the show. The sets, the design, the decor is absolutely stunning from start to finish. The whole concept is really appealing and beautiful. But it doesn't translate into the show really. Not particularly fun. I went once and the stage broke down multiple times during the show. It was hard to enjoy and be engaged, even for the really amazing parts. It's reaching for the same flair and spectacle as other Cirque shows, but never really quite gets there. I'd consider it for the theatre experience. Otherwise, I'd go see another show.

I bought a used mechanical keyboard for $38. It is a decent price, you get decent stuff for that. It's very rattle. When you hit the spacebar, it rattles like a tray of cutlery, so I just learn to ignore it. My fingers know when I've actually hit it. Each key has a stop, a little bump partway down, so I know I've pressed the key. I can type an email and my hands feel fine after. That's why I'll keep it. The E key repeats now and then, so I have to reread everything before sending. It happens maybe once every few paragraphs, so it's not a big deal. I asked the seller what switches it had. I got tired of waiting, so I just bought it anyway. I only got the answer a week later, so it's already on my desk. Brown switches. So it stays. I thought about sending it back, but return shipping was going to eat a lot of the money I paid for it, so I'll just live with the rattle.

Bought this used mechanical keyboard for $38 and it is a good keyboard, and I think I got my money's worth, maybe a bit more. It rattles. The space bar rattles. You press it with your thumb and it just rattles like the keys, kind of like a tray of cutlery being nudged. I just tune it out during the day. After midnight it's harder to tune it out, so I start typing around it. The E key repeats now and then, so if I type the word meeting it becomes MEEETING. Maybe once every few paragraphs. It's rare enough that I forget, frequent enough that I have to re-read everything before I send it. I messaged the seller to ask what switches it was, got tired of waiting and just bought it anyway. Got the answer a week later when it was already on my desk. Brown switches for the record. I'm keeping it for the comfort. Each key has a little bump part way down, so your fingers know that you pressed it, but don't slam it to the bottom. I can get through a long email and my wrists are fine afterwards, which the laptop never managed. I considered sending it back, but the return shipping would have eaten a real chunk of what I paid for it, and I would be back on my laptop. So it stays. With the rattle and all.

I recently saw this theatrical circus style show in Vegas and I recommend it, but I’m knocking off a star. The story is sometimes hard to follow and some of the music is sleepy or just not a good fit for the action. But the performers are fantastic, athletic, fit, and have crazy aerobic skills. The girls in particular are very impressive, staying underwater for minutes at a time. The theatre is circular, as is the stage, so you can see it from anywhere. There are three entrances to the stage that are used throughout, and become really important during transitions. The stage and the set and the lighting are really lovely and memorable. The prices are reasonable compared to O and Love, which are major Vegas productions. I wish it had more effects, particularly fire, but that’s not a serious criticism. I think it’s a great show and I do recommend it, though I’m taking off one star for the story and music.

I recently saw this theatrical circus production in Vegas and recommend it, though I am deducting one star. It is very hard to follow the storyline. Music selections don't really fit the action, and it feels sleepy at times. But the performers are amazing. Their athleticism, their physiques, their aerobic skills are unbelievable. The girls are very impressive. They stay underwater for minutes at a time.

The theater is circular. The stage is circular too, so you get a good view from every seat. They use three main stage entrances and exits, which is really important during transitions in the story. The whole setting is beautiful, the stage, the lighting, it's very memorable. The price is reasonable compared to O or Love. I'd like to see more special effects, fire, etc. But that's not a big deal. I would recommend this show. It's really fun. It's very visual.

I'm not arguing that remote work is broken. If I have self-driven devs, remote can be great. If you are a junior and you can't work from home, you're in a disadvantage. It's a huge disadvantage. I've mentored 5 junior engineers over the last two years, and it's been pretty consistent. Remote work is being presented as the fix for everything. But the fact of the matter is, it's not the solution to everything. It's very overblown.

Juniors don't need tickets, documentation, or meetings. They need to sit in on design conversations. They need to watch others debug. They need to ask questions before they have spent hours confused. That kind of interaction happens organically in an office. Remote work requires them to know when to cut in, when to schedule a call, and how to explain a problem they don't fully understand. That's a hard skill to have before you learn it. I've seen the feedback issues. Short comments in code review can feel like the final word instead of a learning opportunity. It takes longer, so less momentum.

The juniors I mentored improved faster if they had pairing, whiteboard sessions, and easy access to seniors. I'm not against remote work. But for juniors, proximity is a booster that gives confidence, context, and instincts. Sending a junior off with a laptop and a calendar can be a drag on junior development, which can result in less good technical leadership in the future.

I think remote work is a bit of a panacea. I know it's not bad, I think it's a great system for self-driven devs. But it's very overblown for junior engineers who are still learning how to code.

The mixer drone, humming low, hummed and hummed, vibrating through the soles of Elias's boots. Flour dust hung in the air like suspended snow, catching the harsh fluorescent light. It was 3:17 AM. The sourdough loaves rested on wooden boards, their crusts still pale and soft before final bake. He wiped his hands on his apron, the fabric stiff with dried dough and sweat. Elias moved to the front counter to check the lock, a ritual born of paranoia rather than necessity. There it sat. The History of Salt. Hardback, blue spine cracked near the hinge. It had appeared every Thursday for six weeks, always placed precisely on the glass display case beside the unsold cinnamon rolls. No library stamp indicated it belonged here; the bakery was not a branch of the municipal system. Elias picked it up. The cover felt cold. He opened it, expecting blank pages or perhaps a forgotten bookmark. Instead, a folded square of lined notebook paper slipped out, landing on the counter with a soft tap. He unfolded it. The handwriting was jagged, pressed hard into the fiber. You knead with your left hand dominant, stop favoring the right, it ruins the tension. Elias stared at the words. The mixer ticked over to the next cycle. He looked at his own hands, red-knuckled and dusted white. He closed the book and placed it back on the glass, aligning the spine perfectly with the edge. Then he turned off the overhead light above the display, leaving the book in shadow.

It was 3:17 in the morning and the mixer was running that low steady hum that you could feel it through the soles of your boots. There was flour dust hanging in the air, catching the fluorescent lights like it was snow. The sourdough loaves were resting on wooden boards and they were still pale and soft. I wiped my hands on my apron, which was stiff from dried dough and sweat. I walked over to the front counter and checked the lock. I do this every time. It’s more paranoia than anything. And there it was, The History of Salt. Hardback, blue spine cracked near the hinge. This book had appeared every Thursday for six weeks, sitting right on the glass display case next to the cinnamon rolls that weren’t sold. There was no library stamp on it. This wasn’t part of the municipal library system. I picked it up. The cover felt cold. I opened it expecting it would be blank pages or maybe a bookmark. But a folded square of lined notebook paper fell out onto the counter and tapped it. I unfolded it. The writing was jagged and pressed hard into the fiber. The note said that I knead with my left hand dominant and stop favoring my right because it ruins the tension. I just looked at the words. The mixer ticked over to the next cycle. I looked at my own hands, red knuckled and white dusted. I closed the book and put it back on the glass, making sure the spine was perfectly aligned with the edge. Then I turned off the overhead light above the display so the book was in shadow.

So I'd say Apple needs to be mentioned. I've just had lots of problems. At my school, they only had Apple laptops for the middle and high schools, which are expensive, two times the price of the PC ones. And they were super flaky. I never dropped my laptop but had to replace the hard drive five times in four years, and reinstall the OS like three times. And a friend's MacBook Pro caught fire while he was watching a movie. It set off the smoke alarm, and it was super terrible. And then Apple support was not great, they couldn't diagnose the problem and just kept backing up the computer and wiping it and restoring it. Then, I had the first iPhone, which was super flaky and would do some random things. And then now they're releasing a new iPhone every two months, and it's just the camera is slightly better. So I'll give them one credit: iPads are the best tablets. I think in time Android will catch up, but right now, iPads are the best tablets.

Apple has to be included, and my personal experience says so. My school only let us Apple kids use Macs in middle and high school. The Macs were almost double the cost of PC alternatives. They broke down roughly once a month. I never dropped my laptop and yet I replaced the hard drive 5 times in 4 years and repeatedly reinstalled the OS. A friend's MacBook Pro actually caught fire once, smoke alarm and all, while he was watching a movie. Apple support kept failing to diagnose the issue, just backed up the computer, wiped it and restored the files. Same with the phones. I owned the very first iPhone and it kept breaking. Apple puts out a new iPhone about every 2 months these days, with just a slightly better camera. I'll give them one concession, qualified. The iPads are the best tablets right now. But Android tablets will catch up eventually.

I just watched Awakening at Wynn Las Vegas. Its fine, but its not really a must-see Vegas show that I would build a trip around. I have been taken to Vegas constantly since I was a kid. I saw tons of shows before I was 21. So I have a pretty good baseline for what these shows can be. And I have seen them all.

The good news is the circular stage is actually smart. From basically any seat, you have a good view. That is not always the case. And if you are staying at Wynn or Encore, there is a good deal. Tickets are normally 125 dollars but 99 for hotel guests. So that is nice.

Some of the individual feats are really cool. The performers are really strong. The aerialists, the acrobats, all that. But a lot of them are feats I have seen in Cirque du Soleil or other shows. But the biggest problem for me was the story, or lack thereof. Its unclear, its weak, its nonexistent. I dont know what they were trying to say. And too much is going on at once. Too much visual, too many pieces moving, too many things trying to be wow. And if anything, I think it would work better with less.

Otherwise, except for a couple of cool stunts, its just a standard, average show. Its not blowing me away. The people I was with were not overwhelmed. But a couple of my friends did like it. So if you have not seen it, do it. Especially if you have the Wynn or Encore deal. But I would not see it again. And I would not pay full price again. It tries to be this giant flashy Vegas show where more is better. But more was just more messy, for me.

I was brought to Vegas all the time. I saw a lot of shows before I turned 21. I have an idea of what these productions can be. Its fine, but not a must see in Vegas. I would not build a trip around it. The circular stage is really clever. From almost any seat, you get a decent view. That is rare in these big shows. If you stay at the Wynn or Encore, you can get tickets for 99. Normally they cost 125. I think the individual acts are really good. The performers are strong. Aerialists and acrobats, etc. But I have seen these things done as well in Cirque du Soleil shows. The story is unclear. It is not there. I do not really understand what it is trying to say. There is too much going on. Too many visuals, too many moving pieces, too many attempts to wow. I think less would be more. But with the few cool stunts aside, it was just a regular show. I was not blown away. The people I was with did not seem to be overwhelmed. Some of my friends did enjoy it, so if you have never seen it, go. Especially if you get the Wynn and Encore deal. But I would not see it again or pay full price a second time. It tries to be this stereotypical big flashy Vegas show where more is better. But to me, more was just messier.

Bought a skateboard at Zumiez, then went back for the rest of my stuff. At first it felt good. My friend, his little brother, and I sat with a lady who introduced herself as a manager. She said she'd been putting boards together every day she worked there, and that on her bad days she'd snapped at customers. I thought it would be quick. Fifteen minutes, at most. But it took ninety. She ruined two bolts, then swapped them for ones that looked like they might be sold to someone else. She finally got her brother and another guy - another manager apparently - to help finish it off. No apology. They've lost our future business. It really broke my heart.

I bought a mechanical keyboard second-hand, it was $38. It has been a chaotic but surprisingly good experience. The seller was really bad at communication. I asked them about the switch type before buying, they took a whole week to answer my message. They answered with one word. So I gambled and ordered it. The board is very well loved. It has a rattle, the space bar is loose, it rattles really annoyingly, it's like a loose Lego brick. The E key occasionally repeats, so I get typos like theee instead of the. It's funny. I love typing on it, it's super comfortable. Tactile, very good. I send out emails, long emails, very long emails, very painful emails. And it's really comfortable to type on. I almost returned it, but it's heavy, it's a slab of plastic. So shipping it back would be a pain. And for $38, it's not worth it. So I decided to keep it. It's a budget win, provided you don't mind a bit of DIY tuning and the occasional double-typing letter.

I picked up this mechanical keyboard used for 38 dollars. Its been a weird ride but it's not bad at all. The seller was a nightmare to deal with, they were a week in responding when I asked them what switch type it had. Told me "tactile" and I had already bought it on a gamble. The keyboard itself is in a very used state. It rattles like hell. The space bar rattles like a lego brick inside. It's really annoying. And then I have a bug where the E key will double type itself, so I'll type "the" and it'll be "theee" and it's very funny. But the thing is I really love typing on it. The feel is really nice, its comfortable for typing out those long, painful work emails. I thought about returning it, but to ship back a heavy slab of plastic for 38 dollars is more work than it's worth. So I'm going to keep it and I've grown fond of its flaws. If you don't mind a bit of DIY work, a little tweaking and a double lettering now and then, its a bargain.

I'm angry.
Beware of Turkish Airlines.
I booked Harbin to Beijing and Turkish Airlines Beijing to Istanbul.
My Harbin flight was delayed and I missed my connection.
No one at the airport booth took responsibility or helped me rebook.
I spent the night in the airport.
Next morning I asked for a ticket.
They said flights were overbooked and it might take days to get to Istanbul, unless I paid for business.
I needed Istanbul so I was forced to accept.
I'm in complete disbelief.

Travelers, Turkish Airlines is a real problem. I got caught in the worst case scenario. I took a domestic flight from Harbin to Beijing, then Turkish Airlines from Beijing to Istanbul. My first flight got delayed and I missed the connection. The folks at the airport booth at the airport would not take responsibility for anything. I had to spend the night at the airport. Next morning, I asked for a ticket. They said flights were overbooked, that I could be in Istanbul for days unless I paid for business class. I needed to be in Istanbul, so I was forced to accept. I'm furious, and I'm in disbelief.

The float valve handles trough filling. Its float is buoyant. When water drops, float sinks, so the valve opens, letting water in. As water rises, float rises and valve closes gradually. At set level, it shuts off and fills stop. For overflow, its two common causes: the valve closes not fully. Debris or mineral buildup, or the float is too high, so it's set too high. And the valve closes after the trough is already overflowing.

How do we avoid overfilling? You need a float valve to control the trough. It uses a float on a lever connected to the valve. Water level drops, the float drops, valve opens. Water fills up, float rises, valve closes. When it's at the set level, the valve shuts off. So it stops. Two common reasons for overfilling is debris or mineral buildup at the valve so it doesn't fully close. Or the float is adjusted wrong, too high, so it will shut off after it's already overflowed.

Siphons are a really cool way to move water. Essentially, you have a tube with a bend, and water wants to fall. It's the weight of the water on the outlet end that pulls it down. To get water into the tube, you've got to fill it with water. What happens is the lower column of water is heavier than the higher column of water. So it has more weight, and it's being pulled down. So it'll pull water out of the source, and it'll pull water up over the crest of the siphon. So the net effect is to move water from one container to another. If you put air in the tube, it breaks the column of water. And as soon as you break the column, the pressure equalizes and the water stops moving. It's pretty amazing. It's like a chain reaction. And if you look at the tube, there's a pressure differential. There's lower pressure in the top of the tube, and the atmosphere pushes water up into the tube. If the outlet is higher than the source, the lower column of water is no longer heavier, and it's no longer being pulled down, and the process stops.

A siphon works by using gravity and air pressure to move water from one container to another over a barrier. First, you have to fill the tube completely with water, making one continuous column. Gravity pulls the water down the longer leg. As water drops down, the pressure at the top of the hump drops. Air pressure on the source container pushes more water up the short leg to fill that low-pressure spot. This keeps water flowing.

The exit end has to be lower than the water level at the start. The force is the weight difference between the two water columns. If the exit is higher or even, gravity pulls down with less force than the force needed to push water up the intake side. The net pull only exists if the side that flows out has more weight than the side going up.

Air gets in, it breaks the continuous column. The connected chain of water molecules is broken. Inside pressure now matches outside. Then the pressure difference that drives the flow stops. So the siphon will fail. You have to fill the tube with water again, remove the air, and the siphon will start working again.

The sourdough was on its second rise when I found it. Again.
It's always a Thursday. It's always right on the flour bin. And it's always a copy of The Count of Monte Cristo with the Richmond Public Library stamp. I don't know how they get past the squeaky screen door without me hearing them, but honestly, around 3am, my brain is mostly yeast and caffeine anyway.
Tonight, though, there was a scrap of yellow legal paper poking out of the top like a bookmark.
I wiped my hands on my apron, leaving a ghostly white smudge on the dark cloth. I pulled the note out. Page 142, it said, in frantic spiky handwriting. Please. I think they're watching the drop box now.
A cold draft swept through the kitchen, smelling of wet asphalt and oncoming rain. I looked toward the darkened front windows, but only saw my own tired reflection staring back.
I didn't open the book. I carefully tucked the note back between the pages. I slid the novel into a brown pastry bag, and folded the top down twice to seal it.

The sourdough was on its second rise. It was on the flour bin, it was a copy of Monte Cristo, with a Richmond Public Library stamp. It's always a Thursday, always at 3 AM. I never hear the squeaky screen door. My brain at 3 AM is basically yeast and caffeine. But tonight, there was a scrap of yellow legal paper poking out of the top of the book like a bookmark. I wiped my hands on my apron, which was dark, and I left a ghostly white smudge on it. I pulled the note out. Page 142, it said, in spiky, frantic handwriting. Please. I think they're watching the drop box now. I didn't open the book. A cold draft swept through the kitchen, smelled of wet asphalt and oncoming rain. I looked toward the darkened front windows. But all I saw was my own tired reflection staring back at me. I carefully tucked the note back between the pages. I slid the novel into a brown pastry bag and folded the top down twice to seal it.

I bought this used mechanical keyboard for $38 and, honestly, I think I got about $38 worth of keyboard. Maybe a little more.

Let's start with the flaws. The space bar rattles, this hollow loose clatter every time my thumb hits it, like a tray of cutlery. I stopped noticing during the day, but late at night it sounds louder than it has any right to. The E key also repeats itself once every few paragraphs, so meeting becomes meeeting. Just often enough to keep me proofreading. Communication with the seller was slow. I asked what switches it used before buying, and it took a week to get an answer, after the keyboard had already arrived. Brown switches for the record.

Still, here's the surprising part. It's genuinely comfortable. The keys have a satisfying cushioned feel. I can write long emails and my wrists don't complain. That's more than I can say for the flat laptop keyboard I was using before. I did consider shipping it back, but the hassle wasn't worth it. So it stays on my desk, rattling, repeating, and quietly earning its keep.

Three stars.

Spent $38 on a used mechanical board. You get what you pay for.

I'll be honest, it's got issues. The spacebar rattles. Not a little rattle, it's this awful hollow clunk. Like you're knocking around a tray of cutlery. I stopped noticing it in the day but it's very prominent at night. I also have trouble with the letter E. Every few paragraphs I'll type "meeeting" and I have to go back and fix it. It's annoying.

I did try to contact the seller about the switches. I asked before buying and got a response a week later, the board was already here. Turns out they are browns.

It is comfortable. The keys have a cushioned feel. I can write long emails and my wrist doesn't hurt. My laptop keyboard is very flat, so there's a difference.

I thought about returning it but it's very light and small, so I didn't want to pay the extra shipping. So it stays on my desk. I type on it all the time. Rattles, repeats, but it's working. It earns its keep. Three stars.

Hi everyone, thanks for having me. So I'm Tom's brother, and we grew up in the same bunk bed until he was 14, so I've been around him for a long time. I remember his loud snoring, fighting over the top bunk. You can see the signs of his character even then. He turned out to be a really reliable guy. Tom is the person you can count on. I forgot my passport once and he drove 6 hours just to get it to me. That's the type of brother he is. Loyal, generous, willing to drive a totally unreasonable distance to save you from your own stupidity. Anyway, Tom. We're happy that you've found someone who loves you the way we do. Old school attendance registers offer historians a window into daily life patterns that official narratives often overlook. They show which kids were there, how often they came, and occasionally why they didn't. This lets historians guess at seasonal work demands, sickness, weather, poverty, home duties, or local disasters. Registers might also display differences between boys and girls, kids of different ages, neighborhoods, or classes, helping researchers see how schooling fit into work, family routines, and community expectations. Study these over many years and you can see shifts in schooling habits or public health. But there is a limitation. Registers just show what the school decided to note. They don't tell you how the kids actually felt or experienced things, and absences could be misreported or missing, or reflect teachers' assumptions. So you really need to compare them with other sources.

Historians really value the old school attendance registers. They can reconstruct patterns of daily life that official narratives have missed. The registers show which kids were there or not. The register shows how regularly they attended and sometimes why they missed school. From that we can infer seasonal labor demands, illness, bad weather, poverty, family responsibilities, migration, local emergencies. Registers also show differences by gender, age, neighbourhood, social class. This helps understand how education fitted into work, household routines and community expectations. If we study them over a number of years we can see how schooling habits and public health changed. They are pretty limited, though. They only record what the school chose to write down. They don't tell us about the children's experiences in detail. Absences may be misreported or incomplete or shaped by teachers' assumptions. But if you use other sources to compare them it works really well.

For this class project, we were testing different folded cardboard bridges. We made some beam, arch, and triangular folded bridges out of the same cardboard. The sizes weren't exactly the same for each one. We put them on two supports, then added weights until they bent or tipped. We only did a few tests in the classroom, and by hand, so we can't really say it's engineering data, so it's not very rigorous. But the triangular folded ones seemed to hold weight more steadily. The geometry of the fold makes them more stable. So the geometry of the fold is the key here.

This classroom project compared the stability of several folded cardboard bridge designs using simple materials and controlled tests. Students built short beam, arch-inspired, and triangular-fold bridges from the same cardboard, keeping length and width as consistent as possible. Each bridge was placed between two supports and small weights were added gradually to see how they bent, tipped, or collapsed. The project was limited by handmade construction, a small number of trials, and classroom testing conditions, so the results should not be treated as engineering data. Overall, the triangular-fold designs held weight more steadily. This suggests that fold geometry can influence stability in model bridges.

I live in Toronto now and no longer use Hydro Ottawa. I am telling you about their alarming billing practices. I held an account for one year when I was renting a downtown apartment. Then I moved back in with my parents to go to school for my masters and I cancelled my account and paid my outstanding charges. And yet, they just kept draining my separate bank account at random intervals for over a year. I phoned customer service and emailed screenshots of the withdrawal but they kept insisting that my account was closed, and that the debits were not happening. It turned out that when I mentioned moving back in with my parents, they linked my banking details to my parents' billing number. That is why they were debiting my account. My parents didn't even notice because they were getting refunds for overpayment. So they thought it was normal. After hours on the phone with different representatives, a manager actually looked into it and confirmed the error and fixed it. But they initially refused to refund the money, and only offered an apology. I will never again give my banking details for automatic debit. I think Hydro Ottawa should be concerned about how they treat personal data and billing.

It just feels stuffy to me. I think it has to do with the humidity. You can be comfortable at 70-72 degrees, but if it is humid, it feels heavy. So, if there is no air movement, no ventilation, the carbon dioxide and odors and the heat that we release is just accumulating in the room. It feels very close. So, just because it's 72 degrees and it's A/C, it's not necessarily less humid. It's not necessarily moving the air. So you open a window, you turn on a fan, you have ventilation, it feels much fresher.

Even when temperature is comfortable, a room can feel stuffy. Humidity plays a big role. If humidity is high, the body can't get rid of heat. The sweat just stays on the skin. A lack of airflow is another issue. Without movement, the CO2 that we're breathing out stays in the room. So it feels very close, it feels very oppressive. Air conditioning cools it but doesn't necessarily reduce humidity. It doesn't necessarily increase airflow. So just opening a window, running a fan, or running ventilation will help make the room feel fresher.

A lot of people think remote work is a win-win. I've mentored five junior engineers for the past two years and I don't think it is. They don't need tickets, docs, or scheduled meetings. What they need is to get in on design arguments, watch somebody else work through a nasty bug, and get answers before the uncertainty snowballs. In the office you get all that for free. From home, they have to figure out when to interrupt, arrange a call, and explain a problem they likely don't yet understand. Asking a beginner to manage all that is a pretty steep ask.

I've seen it really hurt feedback. Short notes on a code review end up sounding like a final judgment, and the lag in getting answers kills forward motion. The people I've worked with moved ahead much quicker when they could pair up in person, work through things on a whiteboard, and actually get hold of the seniors. This doesn't mean scrap flexibility. It works for people who direct their own efforts. For a beginner, being around other people is what gets them there. That's how they pick up the confidence, context, and judgment they need. If you just hand a newcomer a laptop and a calendar, you are going to end up with weaker technical leadership down the road.

So a rain gauge is super simple really. You just have rain falling into an opening of known area and it reports the result as a depth, in millimetres or inches. The depth tells you how much water would cover the ground if none of it drained away, evaporated, or got soaked in. Most gauges use a funnel with a wide opening that feeds into a narrow tube. You know the same amount of water will go higher in a narrow tube so it's easier to read small amounts. But the scale on the tube is marked to account for the area ratio so you get the true rainfall depth. So wind is a big source of error. Because of wind gusts, rain will go past the opening, so it undercounts the rainfall. And evaporation, or splashing before you read it can distort the results.

You can use a simple rain gauge to measure the rain that's fallen over a period of time. It is essentially a bucket with a known area. It reports the result as a depth, usually in millimeters or inches, which is the depth of water that would be left on flat ground if it didn't drain off or evaporate or soak into the ground. Many rain gauges are actually a funnel with a wide opening, but it then feeds into a much narrower tube. Because the same volume of water will rise higher in a narrow tube, it's easier to get a good reading of small amounts of rain. The scale on the tube is marked to account for the area ratio, so you're still reading the true rainfall depth. Wind can be a problem, where it can blow raindrops past the opening and you get an undercount. Also, evaporation or splashing can distort the results before you get a reading.

I really like the old attendance registers. They are pretty much the main material for understanding what people in communities were doing every day. The registers just record attendance. But they show patterns that are caused by the season and agriculture, epidemics, and weather. For example, a sudden drop in attendance might mean the flu is going around, or that people need to work the harvest, so the kids have to be there. So it shows that trade-off. The float valve connects to a pressurized water line. On the water surface, there is a plastic ball or block that floats. It is connected to a lever arm. When the cows drink and the level drops, the float will lower. Then the lever arm is tilted, pulling the plunger or washer away from the valve seat. So water will flow into the trough. When the water goes up, the float rises. The lever pushes the plunger back into the seat, and it gradually closes the opening until the flow stops. The valve is set at a level. When the water is constantly overflowing, it is common that the washer is worn or has debris on it, and it cannot seal properly. Also, if the float is punctured and waterlogged, it won't rise enough to close the valve.
